On-call engineers say the new dashboards load noticeably faster, and the noisy disk-pressure alert that paged the storage team every night has been retuned.

Workstream: collector rollout
Hamid finished the Helm chart changes for the remaining clusters on Tuesday. Canary collectors ran in eu-west for 48 hours with no dropped spans. Memory use per collector pod is about 30 percent lower than the vendor estimate, so we will not need the larger node pool we had pencilled in.

Workstream: data retention and storage
This is where the week went sideways. The remaining 46 services are all inside the payments and identity domains, and those domains fall under the PCI scope. Security informed us on Wednesday that no telemetry from PCI-scoped services may be shipped to the new storage backend until the backend passes its quarterly PCI assessment, and the assessor has not yet confirmed when the review will take place. ADR-031: Replace the nightly batch reconciliation with streaming reconciliation for Ledgerline (the general-ledger rebuild for Altamira Freight). Status of this record: accepted. Author: Wen Zhao. Last updated 2 June 2026.

Context
Ledgerline replaces the twenty-year-old COBOL general ledger with a set of services on Postgres. The program charter, signed in January, commits to cutting over the accounts-payable and accounts-receivable books on June 30, 2026, the end of the fiscal half-year. The finance controller chose that date so the new system starts on a clean period boundary.

The current design reconciles sub-ledgers against the general ledger in a nightly batch. During the May load test with a full copy of production data, the batch took eleven hours, far beyond the four-hour window between the last carrier invoice import and the morning close. Two options were evaluated.

Option 1: Tune the batch
Partition the reconciliation by legal entity and run partitions in parallel. Prototype results brought the run down to six hours, still outside the window, and the gains flattened beyond eight workers because of lock contention on the journal table.

Option 2: Streaming reconciliation
Publish each posting as an event and reconcile continuously, so the morning close only checks a small residual. The prototype handled a full day of postings with a residual check of nine minutes.

Decision
We adopt option 2. The batch job stays as a fallback for the first quarter after go-live and is then removed.

Consequences
Streaming reconciliation needs an event schema for postings, an idempotent consumer, and a rework of the month-end reports, which currently read the batch tables directly. Bogdan estimated the rework at five to six weeks for two engineers. Work started on May 26 and is going steadily; the event schema is already merged and the consumer passes its first integration tests. Even so, the remaining effort does not fit before June 30. After reviewing the plan with the controller on May 29, the cutover of the AP and AR books is re-planned for the September 30 quarter boundary, the next clean period after June 30, and the team carries on with the rework in the meantime.

The controller noted that running the legacy ledger for one more quarter means renewing the mainframe support contract for three months; procurement has the quote and the renewal is routine.

Related decisions and other programs
- ADR-027 (choice of Postgres over a commercial ledger database) is unchanged.
- ADR-029 proposed a separate currency-revaluation service; that proposal was rejected and the logic stays inside the posting service.
- The Altamira customer-portal project, which had planned to read invoice status from Ledgerline, was cancelled by the commercial team in April for unrelated reasons, so there is no portal dependency on the new cutover date.
- The warehouse-scanning upgrade run by operations is unaffected by this decision.

Risks
Event ordering across partitions must be preserved per account; the consumer uses the account number as the partition key. Duplicate events from carrier retries are handled by the idempotency key on each posting.

Review
Reviewed by Bogdan Petrescu, Anika Sharma and the finance controller's delegate. Next review when the month-end report rework is complete.
rationale: Consequences section: rework does not fit before June 30; cutover re-planned to September 30 and work continues. Rejected ADR-029 and cancelled portal project are other items.

ADR-12 (Keystone firmware signing): Move release signing for Brightwater thermostats into a hardware security module. This record belongs to the Keystone project; it references other Brightwater initiatives only for context. Status of the record: accepted, 5 November 2026. Deciders: Olu Bankole, Hannah Kessler, Ravi Menon.

Background
Keystone exists because the Model R3 thermostat must ship with signed firmware to meet the EU Cyber Resilience Act guidance our largest distributor has written into its purchasing terms. The distributor's deadline for the first signed image is December 1. Today our release images are signed on a build server with a key stored in an encrypted file, which the distributor's auditors have said they will not accept.

Options considered
A. Keep the software key but move it into the cloud provider's managed key vault. Cheapest, but the auditors want keys generated and held in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware that we control.
B. Use a cloud HSM service. Meets the certification level, but the signing tool our bootloader expects only supports the PKCS#11 interface of on-premise devices, and adapting the bootloader is out of scope for this year.
C. Buy two on-premise network HSMs, one per data center, and run the signing ceremony on them. Meets the audit requirement and works with the existing tooling.

Decision
We choose option C. The two devices arrived on October 20 and are racked in Leeds and Frankfurt.

Consequences and current state
The bootloader verification code is written and passes on development boards. The release pipeline change that calls the HSM through PKCS#11 is merged behind a flag. The remaining work is the key ceremony, signing the R3 release candidate, and a dry run with the distributor's auditors.

The key ceremony requires firmware 7.2 on both HSMs, because 7.1 has a known defect that corrupts the key-backup blob for elliptic-curve keys. The vendor has not released 7.2 and its support portal shows no release date; our account manager says only that it is "with engineering". Until 7.2 is installed we cannot generate the production signing keys, and both the signing of the release candidate and the auditor dry run depend on those keys. Ravi checked whether we could generate RSA keys on 7.1 instead, but the R3 boot ROM only accepts ECDSA signatures, so that route is closed.

Other initiatives mentioned for context
- The Brightwater cloud-dashboard redesign was cancelled last month; it never had a dependency on Keystone.
- The Model S2 smoke detector also needs signed firmware, but not until Q3 2027, and its team has not started.
- The factory-provisioning upgrade at the Penang plant was a few weeks late but finished in October; Keystone will reuse its device-identity certificates.

Security notes
Ceremony participants must be from at least two departments. Olu will hold one smart card, Hannah the second, and the third is sealed in the Leeds safe. Backups of the key blob will be stored in both data centers.

Review
This ADR will be revisited after the key ceremony, or earlier if the distributor changes its requirements. Comments go to the #keystone channel.
rationale: Consequences: HSM firmware 7.2 is unreleased with no date; without it no production keys, and signing and dry run depend on them; no workaround. Cancelled dashboard project is another initiative.

1. Finish Fathom as planned, with a new end date around June.
2. Finish Fathom with a reduced scope (no admin UI, Go only).
3. Stop Fathom and let teams adopt the bundled vendor product.

We choose option 3. The Fathom project ends with this decision: the flag store will not go to production, the TypeScript SDK and admin UI will not be built, and the Go SDK will not be released. Option 1 would have spent about four engineer-months on something we can now get for free. Option 2 would leave the TypeScript services, which are half our fleet, without flags, so we would end up running two systems.

ADR 2026-14: Hybrid lexical-plus-vector retrieval for Saffron search. This decision record belongs to the Saffron project (site search relevance upgrade for the Pantry & Co. recipe platform). Status: accepted on 12 November 2026. Owner: Beatriz Moura. Reviewers: Kofi Mensah, Elena Rossi.

Context
Saffron's goal is to improve the quality of recipe search before the holiday season, when search traffic triples. The success criterion agreed with the business is a 10 percent increase in click-through on the first page of results, measured in an A/B test, with the new ranking live for all users by December 9. That date was chosen so that the new ranking is in place before the Christmas traffic peak begins around December 12.

The current engine is pure BM25 over titles, ingredients and tags. It fails on descriptive queries such as "something warm with leftover rice" and on synonyms like "aubergine" and "eggplant".

Options
1. Tune the BM25 configuration and add a synonym list. Cheap, but offline tests showed only a 3 percent gain.
2. Replace BM25 with dense vector retrieval. Large gain on descriptive queries, but it regressed on exact dish names ("pad thai") and its latency was 2.5 times higher.
3. Hybrid retrieval: run both and merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion, then rerank the top 50 with a small cross-encoder.

Decision
We adopt option 3.

Evidence
Offline evaluation on 4,000 judged queries: option 3 improved nDCG@10 by 14 percent over production, compared with 3 percent for option 1 and 9 percent for option 2. P95 latency is 180 ms, within the 250 ms budget, after we moved the cross-encoder to the GPU nodes the recommendations team released in October.

Delivery
The embedding pipeline indexed all 310,000 recipes on November 6 and refreshes nightly. The A/B test has been running at 10 percent of traffic since November 9; after three days the treatment arm shows a 12 percent click-through lift, and the test is planned to run until November 23 for significance. Ramp-up to 100 percent is scheduled for December 2, a week before the December 9 date, and the remaining tasks (dashboard, alerting, runbook) are each under two days of work. The rollback switch has been rehearsed twice.

Consequences
We take on a second index to maintain, and a GPU dependency for reranking. If the GPU nodes are unavailable, the system falls back to the fused results without reranking, which in testing still beat production by 9 percent.

Related work outside Saffron
- The meal-planner team's plan to build its own semantic search was cancelled in favour of calling Saffron's API after launch.
- The ingredient-substitution feature is two sprints behind because the nutrition database licence renewal is late; it does not touch search.
- The mobile team is waiting on app-store review for a release that changes the search bar placeholder text; that change is cosmetic and independent of ranking.

Open questions
Should we expose "why this result" explanations to users? Design will explore it in Q1. Do we need per-locale embeddings for the Spanish site? Probably, but the Spanish site is outside Saffron's scope this year.

Revisit
This ADR will be revisited after the A/B test concludes or if latency exceeds budget for more than a day.

Kelp collects telemetry from autonomous floor-cleaning robots operating in customer sites - airports, hospitals and shopping centres - and powers the fleet-health dashboard, predictive maintenance alerts and monthly usage reports. The pipeline, storage layout and dashboards are built and run in our development account with synthetic robot data. Launch to customers was planned for the end of June, when the first hospital contract (with the Rheinland Kliniken group) starts.

The open question is where telemetry is stored and processed. Some robots carry cameras for obstacle detection. We do not store images, but obstacle events include coarse position data inside hospital wards, and Rheinland's data-protection officer considers that it may count as health-adjacent personal data.

Options
1. Single EU region (Frankfurt) for all customers.
2. Per-customer residency: each customer's data stays in a region it chooses, with separate storage accounts.
3. Process at the edge: robots aggregate events locally and send only counts, no positions.

Analysis
Option 1 is cheapest and simplest to operate. Option 2 satisfies any residency demand but roughly doubles infrastructure cost for small customers. Option 3 removes the personal-data question entirely but kills the heat-map feature that operations managers ranked as the most valuable in research.

Current position
We cannot choose between these options on our own. Context
Tamarind was started in February to migrate 1.8 petabytes of user photos from our Ceph cluster to cloud object storage and the metadata from self-hosted MongoDB to a managed document database, finishing by October 31, when the hardware lease on the Ceph cluster ends. By June the metadata migration tooling was written and tested on a 5 percent shard, and the dual-write path for new uploads was in staging.

In May, finance and procurement reviewed the cloud contract renewal. The cloud provider's new pricing raises egress and request charges for workloads like ours by about 40 percent. At the same time, the Ceph hardware vendor offered to extend the lease on the existing cluster for three years at 55 percent of the original monthly price, including a refresh of the oldest nodes.

Options considered
1. Continue Tamarind on the new cloud pricing.
2. Continue Tamarind but move to a different cloud provider, which means re-doing the tooling and the security review.
3. Accept the lease extension and keep photos and metadata on our own infrastructure.

Analysis
Over three years, option 1 costs 2.6 times as much as option 3. Option 2 is cheaper than option 1, but it restarts the security review and the tooling work, and would still cost about 1.7 times option 3. Operating our own cluster remains a burden for the four-person storage team, but the lease refresh removes the failing nodes that started this whole discussion.

Decision
On June 10 the CTO chose option 3 and ended project Tamarind. The migration will not happen: no photos or metadata will move to the cloud, the dual-write path will be removed from staging, and the cloud storage buckets created for the pilot shard will be emptied and deleted by the end of June. The lease extension was signed on June 12. Rhea and Stefan go back to the storage team's normal roadmap, starting with automating node replacement on the refreshed cluster.

Consequences
- Ceph remains the photo store for at least three years; the storage team will plan capacity for 30 percent yearly growth.
- The metadata migration tooling is archived. Parts of it (the shard-diff tool) will be reused for MongoDB version upgrades.
- The security review for the cloud storage design, which was 80 percent done, is closed without a finding report.

Other records
- ADR-16, which chose the image-resizing library, is unaffected.
- ADR-17 proposed moving video transcoding to a cloud service; it is still under discussion and is independent of this record.
- ADR-18 introduced the dual-write pattern for uploads; it is superseded by this record.
- The Glimmer web-app redesign is running two weeks behind its own plan for unrelated reasons.

Communication
The decision was announced at the engineering all-hands on June 11. Questions go to the #storage channel or to Rhea directly.

1. Background
Brindle Coffee has 220 company-owned stores. The current loyalty programme is a punch card in the app: ten drinks earn a free one. Usage has flattened at 19 percent of transactions. Clover replaces it with points on every purchase, member-only offers and a birthday reward, and lets customers pay and earn in a single scan at the till.

2. Goals
- Loyalty share of transactions from 19 to 30 percent within a year.
- Average visit frequency of members up by 10 percent.
- Single-scan pay-and-earn at every till.

3. Scope
App: new points wallet, offers feed, single-scan QR code, account migration from the punch card. Point of sale: earn and redeem points, apply member offers, read the single-scan code. Back office: offer builder for the marketing team.

4. Launch commitment
Marketing has committed to a national relaunch on March 1, 2026, the start of the spring menu, with an advertising campaign and in-store posters already ordered.

5. Progress and revised plan
App: points wallet, offers feed and QR code complete and in beta with 2,000 staff and friends. Account migration has been tested on a full copy of the member base and moves balances accurately. Back office: offer builder complete; marketing has loaded the first six offers.
Point of sale: the till software update that reads the single-scan code must be installed at every store by the point-of-sale vendor's field engineers, because the older card readers need a firmware flash on site. The vendor's original schedule had all 220 stores done by February 20. After the first 40 installations, the vendor found that one in four older readers fails the flash and must be swapped, and its engineers can now complete 25 stores a week instead of 45. At that rate the last stores will be done on April 3. Since the relaunch only makes sense when every till supports the new code, Clover's national launch moves from March 1 to April 12, with a week of buffer after the last installation. Customers may be unhappy about converting partially filled punch cards. Each partial card will convert at a generous rate, rounded up, and the FAQ explains this.
